title: How This Entrepreneur Built A $1.5 Billion AI Unicorn In One Year
transcript: I think AI will definitely take jobs. Generally that happens with every technology wave and then people move on to better more intellectual things. [music] >> Jesse Zang, thank you so much for joining me. >> Thanks for having me. >> Well, AI agents are talk of the town. Every [music] other company is creating an AI agent to do some sort of task. But what does that actually mean? >> So at Decagon, we do AI customer service agents. So a simple example would be let's say we're working with a big airline. Then essentially what would happen is every single end user that interacts with the airline can use the AI agent as you know the first point of contact to get whatever they need. And so it's the same as you know calling a concierge or or texting someone and it can book flights for you. It can upgrade your seats. It can answer questions you might have about your loyalty points. And the reason why it's so exciting right now is that AI has now kind of gotten intelligent enough where it just feels like a human and you can have it be available 247 any language and it can do all sorts of things for you. >> Mhm. How did you get the idea for it? Because Decagon, you know, is one of the few AI agent companies that kind of made it big early on. Um, as I said, like now every other startup is trying to find their niche within this AI agent thing. So, how did you get the idea for it? What was the sto What's the story behind it? >> Yeah. So, my my co-founder um who's awesome, Ashwin, he and I have pretty similar approaches to starting companies, which is, you know, we think that whenever there's a big technology shift, and in this case with AI, it just opens the door for a lot of a lot of companies, but really the number of great ideas is usually pretty small. And so, your job as a founder is to try to figure out what those are, ideally at the beginning of the cycle. And the only real way you can do it besides guessing is spent a lot of time with customers. And so what we did at the early days was we went out there, we tried to pack a whole day with meetings talking to all sorts of different sort of like enterprises, right? So it could be tech companies or banks or you know retail stores and so on and we were just exploring. So we were trying to figure out you know what would people find useful? How would they think about the ROI? How would they think about actually making an investment in AI? And you know, we kind of repeated that cycle for a couple weeks, right? You try to have a full day of meetings, hack on stuff during the night, come back the next day like, hey, we built this thing, like is this useful? And that was very helpful. And I think it led us to to figure out that there were a lot of use cases that people were excited about, but at the end of it, they didn't really feel like they had real, you know, like investment opportunities for them to spend money and actually, you know, invest in something. And so for us, we, you know, went through that process and the idea behind Dekon came out of that. So we had a lot of enterprises that were like you know you know this use case would be helpful but really over here we have a thousand people in our contact center it'd be great if you could do something there and so they kept pushing us towards this idea and that's how we we started Decagon >> and are you staying focused on you know customer service customer support or do you think decagon would branch out of that at some point >> eventually? Yeah. So, at the core of what we're doing is we're becoming very good at having conversations. And so, at the core, what Zakugon is, it's it's a conversational AI engine, um, we want to build the smartest and most humanlike and most empathetic agents that can have conversations with with folks. >> In the context of enterprises, um, that can be a lot more than just customer service, right? You can kind of, you know, have proactive conversations. you have conversations to get people more engaged or get them to convert into something or just you know you be like a a partner for for the for the end customer and that's really exciting. I mean that's where we're we're going ultimately and customer service is is the best first starting point and we have very high conviction in that now because it's the it's the use case where people are just like oh yeah I get it you know like I'm spending 50 million right now with Decagon I can spend 10 million so you know it's it's great. Um but eventually we as we expand we've already started talking with a lot of our current customers about other types of conversations we can take on and that's ultimately where we think the industry is going. >> Do you have your own like models that you're training or are you you know working with open AI or anthropic or something like that. >> Uh it's it's a mix of both. >> Okay. >> So we are in the layer of the tech stack called the application layer. And so that's the the sort of final layer that's actually solving business problems or interacting with users. And generally people in application layer like us need to be model agnostic. And so you have to you know use anthropic, use open AI, use Google and and fine-tune your own models. Um why why would you fine your own models? Well, generally it's because you can make things a lot faster and more performant and and use smaller models. And so you know for us for example when we uh build our voice agents and you so you can you can call an agent, it just sounds like a human, it responds instantly. the latency there matters a lot and so that's when you end up you using your own models. >> What makes DecaGon's agents better than the other ones out there? >> So we've taken kind of a a unique approach from the rest of the industry. I think generally you can sum it up by we've made our agents a lot more sort of accessible to nontechnical users to use. >> Okay. >> And generally you know AI is a complex space. you you often have to have you know technical resources engineers coming in configuring the models and the setting it up so that you can do what you want and for us we've just taken the view that you know one of the beautiful things with the AI models is that they've really democratized how people can use them it's it's super easy to communicate with them it's very intuitive and so we built our whole product around that and so far that's been resonating with the market >> yeah I mean $231 million raised at a $ 1.5 billion valuation that's a lot How did that happen? >> Yeah, we we've been very fortunate uh with our investors. They've been great partners with us. >> Raising actually to be honest has not really been something we thought much about when we started the company. Um we never really sought out like sought out funding or went out to raise and when we started Asher and I were kind of in the fortune position. We had you know started exited companies before. We knew a lot of investors personally and so each one of our rounds actually so far has been preempted and you know investors have come to us and been like hey we want to give you money at at this price and and generally we're like no we're not really comfortable with that right now but eventually as our business has grown we at some point are like okay it's time to raise the next round and that's when we do it. >> Okay. >> Um so yeah I think that's maybe a sign of the times with AI right now is very hot and a lot of people just see the potential in it you know us included of course. Um, and so we are we are appreciative of it, but it's not really something we we spend much time thinking about. >> Very interesting. And yeah, it might be this a sign of the times or it might be that I don't know your last company was sold to Google, acquired by Google. Tell me about that first company. >> Yeah, I started the company um right out of college, so I left a year early and um yeah, I just wanted to start a company, but generally when you're a new grad, you're young, you don't really like know what you're doing. And so it was like two years of just like random wandering around and a lot of ups and downs, a lot of just like struggling to figure out what to build and it's very painful at the time. I think it does teach you some things about you know how to evaluate ideas and obviously this time things have gone a lot smoother but you know timing also matters the the idea also matters. Um but eventually I think we were very fortunate. We we launched something that got a lot of traction. We were in the gaming space. So we got acquired by Niantic um which you know spun out of Google. They're the makers of Pokémon Go. >> And so that was also a great experience. Worked with some fantastic people there. And around the time you know GP4 came out and the new wave of AI models we just or I I was a solo founder the first time. Um this time it just felt like okay I can't miss out on this on this wave. >> What what was a gaming startup like? What were you actually doing >> as a company was called Loki? We were doing essentially high performance video capture for games. And so one way we'd often describe it is like Snapchat before your virtual experiences. And so when people are playing games, it's like running and capture clips and you can edit them and share them and and post them and so on. >> And at college, what what were you like studying? I want to know more about Jesse Zang, the person. [snorts] >> Sure. Yeah. So I went to Harvard for college. Uh did computer science. Uh my background was very mathy growing up. So uh when I grew up I grew up in Boulder, Colorado. And I would describe my upbringing and childhood as uh I looked back I had a very happy childhood but it was like fairly hardcore. Credit to my parents I guess. And we yeah we just spent a lot of time you know math competitions and and really just spending time working. And I think that's kind of instilled some of that into us today as well. even into the culture of Decagon where I think we've we a lot of folks you know that honestly have similar upbringings to me where we really have bought into the vision we really like working we believe what we're working in and we we spend a lot of hours and so that was me growing up um and I think a lot of people with mathy backgrounds they end up choosing computer science and and technical >> uh fields that are a little bit more applied and a lot of my friends did go into more theoretical things like math professors and computer science professors and so on but I I even from like you know high school, middle school, I was very sure that I wanted to do something more applied and I saw a lot of you know my older friends from these contests doing companies and having some success and >> uh so it just felt a lot less of like a mythical thing that you could do and I was just like yeah you know you can there's investors you can raise from there's programs you can do and and that's how I got into it. It's one thing to have a really, you know, great technical background and know all these things and have an idea and it's another to run a business. As CEO of Decagon now and as someone who has previously founded and you know sold a company, what have you learned about running a business? >> Yeah, totally agree. By the way, so this is something I actually think about a lot. um through out you know high school, college, I met so many super smart people and honestly building and starting a company is you're kind of using a lot of the same problem solving skills right because there's a lot of these like ambiguous problems that come up and at the end of the day you have to figure out like okay how do you think about the problem how do you figure out a solution and then you solve it and so I think a lot of these like hyper intelligent people that were like you know star academic folks growing up I think could be applied very Well, in this business world, I think generally the thing that's not really taught and >> people I don't think invest in enough is just more of like a I would describe as more of a commercial sense. Okay. >> So, like how do you do sales? How do you find customers? How do you evaluate if like a commercial opportunity is good or not? >> And that's not something you get taught in school. I I don't I would even say you get taught that in business school or anything. It's just something you have to learn from experience or someone has to teach you. And so I I actually think there's a huge amount of untapped talents and potential in that world of like people that were just like super strong at you know math or computer science or or whatever that um you know don't have enough training on commercial things and you know trying to smell out like where the opportunities are how to do sales >> how to do marketing >> and um I was fortunate I had a lot of folks that were very good teachers or mentors who were older founders and so on but also I think I always just enjoyed that sort thing and um yeah I do think there's like a lot of untapped potential there. >> Yeah. I wanted to ask you like who have been some of your mentors in this space whether that those are investors or professors anyone you would you know whether it's one person or a few anyone that's been really pivotal for your career. >> Yeah so there's both the older founders like there's a lot of founders I obviously respect a lot. Um, one of my favorites is Ali from Data Bricks, okay, who has been kind enough to, you know, spend time with us. And I think that that business is just like, you know, one of the best businesses of all time. And they also have like >> one of the just cleanest, sharpest execution styles. Um, and then for for us as a company, so one of our board members, RF from Bane, is yeah, he's been absolutely awesome for us. Um, he started, you know, several companies before. He's been investor for a long time. He's just seen a lot of reps and that's always helpful. Like no matter how smart you are, how smart you think you are as a founder, there's there's like no real replacement for experience and kind of seeing things succeed and fail. And so you have to kind of be mindful of trying to learn from from those folks. >> The value can be pretty cutthroat. How do you think about competition? >> Um I mean I I actually think like any career path is competitive. Yeah, >> competition is fun. Like you need competition to give yourself the fire and give your team a fire to like really push. We have extremely competitive team. Um, one of our, you know, company's principles is like having a winner's mindset and people are here to win. They enjoy winning. They work very hard and a lot of that is rooted in, you know, building something that's a winning culture and a winning product. And yeah, I mean, I think it's it's part of the backgrounds that a lot of the team has as well. I mentioned, you know, growing up doing a bunch of contests and competitions and >> it just gives a lot of the work you're doing a little bit more meaning, I think, because there's results that are measurable and so on. So, I I don't view as a bad thing and I think I would argue that most career paths are pretty competitive anyways. >> Yeah. What's like a typical day at the Decagon office? >> So, we are a fully office culture, which is nice. We have a nice big office in downtown San Francisco and so people show up you know the the go to market folks usually get in a little bit earlier and then engineers will get in a bit later and then stay later and we're just all in sort of like the same space. Um and depending on your role like for me these days it's a lot of you know customer related things a lot of hiring related things and so lots of meetings during the day for the engineers you know we try to protect their time and so they get as much you know just like focused working time as possible but >> everyone in the same space get dinner with each other get lunch with each other you know people you know have a lot of time just like chitchatting >> are you about that you know the nine to9 life the >> oh the [laughter] 996 Yeah, the 996. >> So, I mean, yeah, 996, as you probably know, came from the Chinese companies and my parents are Chinese and I'm ethnically Chinese. So, we actually I've seen a lot of those environments firsthand. I can tell you that in at least in this new AI world where a lot of companies are working really hard, I think it's still another level over there. There's a bunch of reasons. One of the reasons is that um the uh it's much harder to get a job over there. the companies have a lot more leverage. >> So, and I actually don't think it's necessarily the time. I actually don't really believe in enforcing time and and things like that. You want to just build a team that, you know, if they have stuff to do, then they'll push through and do a good job on it. Um, our team, you know, we're in the office 5 days a week. You know, some people come in on the weekends, but it's not required. And that works for us. I mean, other things might work for other companies. Um, I don't think we also want to just have an intense culture to to have an intense culture, right? Like we we want one because people here believe in the mission. They believe what they're working on. >> They enjoy kind of being in a just like in the fire, being like in the center of this new, you know, trend of of AI. And yeah, like you say before, right, there's a lot of companies building, you know, in AI, building in our space. And so part of you know having competition and part of being in a fast growing space is that you know people feel like they can invest the time. It's exciting. They have super smart people they're working on with and ultimately we want everyone who works at Deagon to view this as you know the highlight of their career like they got so much done. >> Uh we made so much progress you know they they were able to accelerate their careers. Do you feel like we are in a time where investors are just kind of throwing money at AI companies that they see have the potential to scale? Like you know, you mentioned that you didn't even seek this out. It came to you and obviously you have the credentials for it, but we see it a lot. We just so much funding has gone into AI these past two three years. As an insider, what's your take? Yeah, I think these cycles are a little bit inevitable because no one can argue that AI is going to be super transformational. But at the end of the day, there's only going to be a small handful of like truly, you know, generational companies. I mean, that's just by definition, but no one knows who who they are, right? Even now, I think it's still super early, so you can't really tell who they are. >> So, as an investor, your job is to try to figure out who they are. Um, and you know, so far it seems like it's been quite easy for a lot of these funds to raise a lot of cash. And if you have a lot of cash, where do you want to deploy the funds? Okay, you're probably going to look towards the AI space because that's where things are happening. And yeah, and that that kind of leads to a little bit of imbalance where there's a smaller set of companies that are doing well and there's a lot of cash and so it's easier to raise. And I don't think that's necessarily good or a bad thing. It really it just means that the founders have to be a little bit more disciplined and try to do things in a more measured way and not just you know blow out the valuation because you can. >> Absolutely. Do you want Decagon to be one of those generational companies? What's your long-term goal with it? Would it be something you want to, you know, see through an IPO or something you would be open to being acquired >> and maybe you haven't thought about it? Yeah, I mean that's not something I would say most founders think about because like >> you're kind of in the thick of it, right? But I would say of course we want to build a generational company. You know, Asha and I have had ex exits before. >> We don't necessarily want to do that again. Like I think we we are in this because we want to, you know, build something huge really have a gigantic win for for our entire team and everyone who's who supported us. So I think we we're in we're very blessed to be in like the right time and have the right opportunity and be working on the right thing um at the moment. So yeah, we just want to keep going. >> I want to know how you know you have some really really big customers. How did you land them especially in the beginning? Was it you going out and like pitching your company or what did it look like? >> Yeah, enterprise sales not super easy. I have learned a lot about it and still a lot to learn. I mean every company can do it differently and what what works for us is that >> when you are selling our agent and working trying to partner with big enterprises around you know their contact center and conversational agents it ends up being a pretty top- down initiative because our customers view this as hey this is our opportunity to have an AI transformation. it's going to be a big bet that we have an AI and you know customer service is a very obvious use case and so let let's go there and as a result it's it's quite important for us to have alignment with the execs of the company and so what's worked for us is we kind of go in we work with the execs we kind of convince them that our approach is the best approach right like you know and as I mentioned before our approach is really rooted around how can you empower and uplevel all the nontechnical users all the business users in your organization >> and people really like that vision right like they might have engineers in the org, but you don't want the engineers on the hook for all these things like you know teaching the AI how to do you know a reorder product or or whatever like all these all these journeys and all these behaviors that you want the AI to learn you want to empower the business users for that and we kind of you know talk them through this vision and really align with their AI strategy and that's how we were able to get off the ground and land some of these customers >> and from there it gets slightly easier because they see oh you know this other company that I respect uses you so you know let's try it out. >> Yeah. Yeah. No, absolutely. What's your give me your best practical advice to other young founders out there that are trying to build and scale companies right now? >> Yeah, I mean I think the the most relevant one is you have to re really understand what your own strengths and weaknesses are. And another way of saying that is maybe try to ignore most advice out there because I think what I found is most advice, most stories. First of all, there's a lot of sort of, you know, polish on those stories that are not necessarily true, right? Like, you know, you want to tell a good story and so you kind of explain what happened, but you're not going to get all the details in it. And so when you listen to other people's stories or other people's advice and learnings, it's kind of a slightly doctorred version of what happened. and it's probably not that applicable to you in the first place because it's a different company, different stage, different founders. And so I think probably the the biggest thing is you need to have like a pretty deep understanding of yourself and what you're good at and where you can actually be you world class at something and that's quite difficult. And so once you kind of build that intuition then you can figure out you know the path that you should take and what type of product you should build and you know what your competitive differentiators are because otherwise it's just super easy to be like oh well you know I saw the story where you know Deagon did XYZ so let's try that or like some other company did XYZ and that can be really distracting because you know it's not really the most relevant thing for your business and I I definitely felt this in my first company where I was very into listening to podcasts and news articles and so on and trying to apply learnings But you know it doesn't really work if it's like a completely different type of business and you know completely different stage and so yeah I think the most important thing is just stay focused and try to understand yourself and your team and go from there. >> Absolutely. I love that you say that you know people shouldn't take other people's advice always. Um, but what's one one business lesson or one one, you know, piece of like ethos that you've kept throughout your entrepreneurial journey? >> For us, it's to always put our customers first. And I mean, this is not a hot take obviously like a lot of companies do this, but we do this very aggressively. We do this even so far as to, you know, determine what things to work on. Even even the idea for the company, right? We we didn't start the company and be like, okay, instantly, you know, customer service agents is the thing to build. We spend a lot of time with customers and I think we've gotten quite good at having those conversations and figuring out, you know, what is the real signal in these conversations and we try to apply that to everything both in terms of how do we develop the product, how do we structure the team and so on. So that that's number one and and number two I would say is just that we have like a really high level of um you know competitive spirit and intensity at Decagon and that served us well so far. >> Um that was the case at my last company as well and just you know I think it just comes from the personalities of the founders like Asha and I are both very competitive and um we have a lot of I would say like fire to just get stuff done and that's you know kind of permeated in the in the team as well. >> Put aside Decagon for a second. What do you want Jesse Zang's legacy to be? >> Hm. I would say, you know, hopefully Jesse has, you know, helped start one of the most consequential companies in the AI era. But honestly, I don't really think too much time think about that. I think that can be for later after career's over. >> After career is over. >> All right. Lastly, do you think AI is going to replace human jobs? I mean you're doing that for a certain you know segment of companies but you know there's a fear instilled in the common individual about AI taking over so >> yeah so I think AI will definitely take jobs and I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing and I don't think there should be that much fear about it because generally that happens with every technology wave a lot of jobs are kind of made redundant because AI can do it faster and better and then people move on do better, more intellectual things, right? So, as an example, you know, in customer service now, a lot of they're called the tier one conversations. So, the easiest conversations can be taken over by AI. And it's not really arguable that AI can do them super well, super consistently, super fast, 247. And I obviously if you're enterprise, you you would want AI to take those, but that doesn't mean that you'll need less humans because there's always more growth opportunities for the businesses, right? And so a lot of the contact centers or or teams that we work with over time what happens is that there's less less and less and less of the workforce doing these tier one tickets but they end up doing other things and you know they could be even outside of customer service like labeling data and things like that. And most of the stories we've seen of people really realizing you know massive gains and massive efficiencies in their operations they're not really firing big swats of people. I mean these these firms usually have you know very high level of churn in these jobs anyways and so they kind of naturally phase out over time into other roles and that's what I think will happen. >> Good. All right. Well, thank you so much for joining me. >> Cool. Thanks for having me. [music] Hey.

title: How Two Self-Made Entrepreneurs Built Global Businesses—and Redefined Success
transcript: Self-made icons, the business of bold ambition, please welcome Anastasia Soare, founder and CEO, Anastasia Beverly Hills. Sonia Gardner, president, managing partner, and co-founder, Avenue Capital Group. And moderator, Moira Forbes, EVP, Forbes. >> All right. So, I'm I'm excited for this conversation because today we've talked about the current state of affairs in the economy, but we're going to chat with two founders who built through it all, all these different types of market cycles, and how they've continued to endure in extraordinary ways. Anastasia, I'll start with you because you arrived in this country in 1989. I read $200 in your pocket. You're child >> No, no, not even. No. >> Not even? >> Not even a coin. Um, and within 3 years, you had built your own salon betting on a market in the US that no one paid attention to, and that was the eyebrows. Fast forward today, it's a multi-billion dollar category, something that you really built in in this country. I would love for you to look back and speak to what is it What did it take for you to build a category that truly didn't exist? And one now that you're working within that is so saturated. >> Well, um, when I arrived in United States, of course, I was an aesthetician and I saw a gap that nobody paid attention to eyebrows. Being trained to see balance and proportion, and and knowing in our classes that golden ratio was so important, I was able to to believe so much into this eyebrows. Why women in United States didn't pay attention to eyebrows? So, not only I had to fix my own eyebrows because I was a victim of the '80s pencil-thin round eyebrows because it didn't exist an Anastasia technique. Um and um I started shaping my own eyebrows. Then I started sharing that with my clients. It was a pure desire to offer that to my clients after I would do before I would do their facials. And I realized that everybody was smiling. I I would see the proportion and balance in what change on their face. So, there were no products for eyebrows. So, I started creating eyebrow products. They were not on the market. And nobody really believed in eyebrows. And um it was a long journey of no, this is not going to work here, but having the salon and and kind of connecting with my customer constantly and creating products that they were for a specific problem, for specific eyebrow, specific colors. I think was the success of my my brand. And it's today as well. And you ask with so much noise right now, how we do it? Well, I think I know eyebrows so much and makeup because for from the beginning, I really wanted to create something that my customer will use and great quality. And And we use it not only once. I wanted a repeated client. >> And I think >> it's so interesting because you were solving a problem that customers didn't even know they had at at that moment in time. Sonia, I'll I'll turn to you. You and your brother started in 1989 uh in a niche that that very few people wanted to try touch, and that was distressed debt. A market that you called inefficient, illiquid, and with very few players at the time. You launched Avenue Capital a few years later. Fast forward today managing billions of dollars across the US, uh Europe, and Asia, and and a multitude of different categories. Take us back to that building phase when so many people were very skeptical and doubtful about the approach that you took and what you learned from that skepticism. >> So, when we started, there was very little competition and and we were able to have an edge. There was couldn't order anything online. We were still typing on typewriters. So, you really could be an entrepreneur and get ahead just in terms of working really hard, but also thinking about how do you get out there first. Right? And for us, it we never imagined it was going to grow the way that it did, but it was something that was very interesting. We're both lawyers back then. Everything filed Chapter 11 and then we would start buying the distressed debt. So, fast forward to today, everything is online, right? You can order everything and and get it in in 10 minutes. And and so, having an edge is a lot different than when we started, but it evolved. It evolved and and as competition grew in what we did, that's when we started Avenue Capital, which was a good move. We know that now, but back then we didn't know exactly how it would turn out, but we wanted to hedge our bets and and also have a distressed debt brokerage business and Avenue at the same time. >> Uh Sonia, I want to go back to to what you were talking about before in terms of how you've continued to to be a thriving product. And what's so interesting your category especially that you've outlasted most brands that have come up alongside you. Right now we're living in a world where you have so much transformation and disruption. Customers buying products through TikTok, a multitude of different different things. What does it take for you to continue to have a brand that stays relevant and connected to a customer in terms of of this marketplace today and in terms of the values of your business? >> Well, I go back. I lived in Romania for 30 years in a communist regime where you you were not sure of your destiny. You didn't know what's going to happen tomorrow. So you had to be adaptable. You had to be resourceful. You had to find ways to solve problems, which I describe being an entrepreneur kind of the same thing. So as myself starting the business, I wanted to be alert. I wanted to try things even if I didn't know because I didn't have the money to to do what I could do today, but I will try little. I will be on every TV show. I will try everything. I wanted to be adaptable and resourceful and I will always ask my client. I was never afraid to say, you know, I don't know. Can you teach me? And I I moved that. I start working. Now the company is a completely different level, but again, I want to be resourceful. I want to find out about AI. How I could use AI and of course always innovation.
